questions.title: Why is a ternary weight model described as "1.58 bits"?
questions.question_body: The paper claims every parameter takes values in {−1, 0, +1} and calls this "1.58 bits". I assume this is because there are 3 states and log2(3) ≈ 1.58496. Is that the correct rationale, and if so, how is this reconciled with practical storage, which usually packs to whole bytes or at least 2 bits? In the implementation, are weights actually stored in 2 bits (wasting some states), and does this affect the claimed memory savings?

questions.title: How is backpropagation performed with ternary weights in BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: The model constrains weights to {−1, 0, +1} via a quantization function. During training from scratch, are the forward weights strictly ternary while the gradients are computed with a straight-through estimator (STE)? If so, what is the exact surrogate gradient used for the RoundClip operation? Are there any tricks (e.g., gradient scaling, clipping, or stochastic rounding) to stabilize training?

questions.title: What is the precise meaning of the absmean scaling in the quantizer?
questions.question_body: The paper defines γ = (1/(nm)) ∑_{ij} |W_{ij}| and uses \(\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma + \epsilon), -1, 1)\). Is γ computed per weight matrix (per layer), per row, per column, or per output channel? Have you compared per-tensor vs per-channel scaling, and how does this choice affect accuracy and the fraction of zeros?

questions.title: How are activations quantized to 8 bits per token and what is Q_b?
questions.question_body: The activations are said to be quantized to the range \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) per token to remove zero-points. How is \(Q_b\) determined in practice (e.g., a running max, a percentile, or learned scale)? Is the scaling computed independently at each layer and time step token, and is the scale stored along with the KV cache for attention?

questions.title: Does BitNet b1.58 use only additions for matrix multiplication in practice?
questions.question_body: The paper says matrix multiplications involve almost no multiplications, relying on integer additions because weights are in {−1, 0, +1}. For a dot-product \(y = \sum_i w_i x_i\) with ternary \(w_i\), we still need to implement \(w_i x_i\) as \(+x_i\), \(0\), or \(-x_i\). On current GPUs/CPUs, isn't this still implemented with integer multiply-accumulate instructions or table/bit operations? Can you clarify what kernels or primitives are used so that actual multiplication is avoided and whether popcount-style tricks are utilized?

questions.title: Why keep embeddings in full precision while quantizing all other weights?
questions.question_body: The results mention that memory scaling is better for larger models because the embedding layer remains full precision and becomes a smaller proportion. Why are token embeddings (and possibly the LM head) left in FP16/BF16 instead of ternary? Have you tried ternary embeddings or 8-bit embeddings, and what was the impact on perplexity and downstream tasks?

questions.title: How are attention-specific computations handled in 1.58-bit LLMs?
questions.question_body: In attention, we have Q, K, V projections and then softmax over scaled dot products. Are Q/K/V projection weights ternary as well, and are the activations quantized to 8 bits before the softmax? Is softmax computed in FP16/BF16 for stability? If activations are per-token scaled to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\), how do you ensure numerical stability of the attention logits and softmax?

questions.title: What accumulator bit-width is used for INT8 additions in matmuls?
questions.question_body: With 8-bit activations and ternary weights, the dot products can sum O(d) terms where d is the hidden size. What integer accumulator width is used to avoid overflow (e.g., INT32)? Is there any scaling or block-wise accumulation to keep sums within bounds, and does this introduce any extra dequantization steps that add latency?

questions.title: Is the quantization function equivalent to a form of weight normalization or L1 regularization?
questions.question_body: Because weights are divided by \(\gamma = \mathrm{absmean}(W)\) before rounding to {−1,0,+1}, this resembles a kind of normalization. Does this implicitly impose a regularization effect similar to weight normalization or an \(\ell_1\) penalty? Is there a theoretical link explaining why introducing 0 improves "feature filtering" and generalization?

questions.title: Are biases completely removed in BitNet b1.58, and why?
questions.question_body: The paper says biases are removed. Is this primarily to simplify quantization and reduce compute/memory, or did biases degrade performance when quantized to ternary? Do you have ablation results comparing with vs without biases in a ternary setting?

questions.title: How is SwiGLU implemented with ternary Linear layers?
questions.question_body: SwiGLU involves two linear projections and a gating nonlinearity. Are both projection matrices ternary and are the intermediate activations 8-bit before the elementwise multiply? Is the elementwise product done in INT8 or temporarily promoted to higher precision, and does that introduce multiplications that break the "almost no multiplication" claim?

questions.title: What exactly is the "2-bit kernel from Ladder" used for ternary weights?
questions.question_body: The runtime measurements use a 2-bit kernel from Ladder even though the weights are ternary (3 states). How are the three states encoded into 2 bits, and is there any wasted state or remapping cost? Does the kernel natively support {−1, 0, +1}, or do you pack as 2-bit and handle mapping in microcode, and how much overhead does that introduce?

questions.title: How precise are the energy savings estimates on 7 nm and which operations dominate?
questions.question_body: The paper cites a 71.4× arithmetic energy saving for matmul based on references for 7 nm. Are these per-operation energy figures for FP16 add/mul vs INT8 add still representative on modern GPUs/NPUs? How sensitive is the saving if, in practice, memory movement dominates energy over arithmetic? Do you include SRAM/DRAM access costs in the end-to-end energy numbers?

questions.title: How is the fairness of the FP16 LLaMA baseline ensured?
questions.question_body: You pre-train both models on RedPajama for 100B tokens. Could you detail the exact optimizer (e.g., AdamW), learning rate schedule, weight decay, gradient clipping, dropout, batch size, and sequence length for both FP16 LLaMA and BitNet b1.58? Were they matched, and did ternary training require special hyperparameters or longer warm-up?

questions.title: What is the distribution of zeros in ternary weights and does it create structured sparsity?
questions.question_body: Since weights can be 0, what fraction of weights become 0 at convergence, and does this vary by layer (e.g., attention vs MLP)? Is there any emergent structured sparsity (e.g., at block or channel level) that hardware could exploit for further speed-ups beyond the ternary arithmetic?

questions.title: How does per-token activation scaling interact with KV cache reuse at inference time?
questions.question_body: If the activation quantization scale \(Q_b\) is computed per token, then the K and V stored in the KV cache presumably need their associated scales to be reused for later attention. Is the scale saved alongside the cached tensors? Could different per-token scales across time cause numerical mismatches when computing attention between old and new tokens?

questions.title: What computations remain in higher precision in BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: Even if Linear layers use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, operations like RMSNorm, rotary embeddings, softmax, and loss are often computed in FP16/BF16/FP32. Which operations are still higher precision in your implementation? Does this limit the theoretical speed-up, and are there plans/feasibility to quantize RMSNorm or softmax safely?

questions.title: How do you prevent accuracy loss from quantizing activations symmetrically without zero-point?
questions.question_body: The paper removes zero-point quantization by symmetrically scaling activations to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\). Many quantization schemes benefit from asymmetric quantization with a zero-point, especially for non-symmetric distributions. Why is symmetric sufficient here, and did you measure the difference in perplexity/accuracy between symmetric vs asymmetric activation quantization?

questions.title: What is the exact scaling law you claim for 1.58-bit LLMs?
questions.question_body: The paper says "BitNet b1.58 is enabling a new scaling law with respect to model performance and inference cost" and provides size equivalences (e.g., 13B 1.58-bit vs 3B FP16). Is there a formal scaling relation or empirical fit (e.g., performance vs compute/memory/energy) you can share? How does this law compare to Chinchilla-like compute-optimal scaling laws?

questions.title: How do latency and memory speed-ups scale with model size and sequence length?
questions.question_body: Figures suggest the speed-up increases with model size because nn.Linear dominates more at scale. Can you quantify how the speed-up depends on hidden size, number of layers, and sequence length? For very long sequences where KV cache dominates memory bandwidth, do the benefits diminish unless KV is also quantized further (e.g., to 4 bits)?

questions.title: How reproducible are the FasterTransformer latency measurements?
questions.question_body: You report latency per output token using FasterTransformer plus a 2-bit kernel. Could you specify GPU model, clock settings, CUDA/cuDNN versions, batch size, input length, output length, and any tensor-parallel/pipeline settings? Is there a public script or config to reproduce the reported 2.71× and 4.1× speed-ups?

questions.title: Why does 3.9B BitNet b1.58 outperform 3B FP16 despite lower precision?
questions.question_body: The results say the 3.9B 1.58-bit model is faster and more memory efficient than 3B FP16 while performing better. Is the improvement mainly from having more parameters, or does the ternary training confer some implicit regularization that helps generalization? Do you have a controlled comparison at exactly the same parameter count?

questions.title: How does training stability compare to FP16 from scratch?
questions.question_body: For from-scratch training with ternary weights and 8-bit activations, did you observe training instabilities (loss spikes, divergence) compared to FP16? Did you need special initialization, longer warm-up, adaptive gradient clipping, or noise injection? Any curves showing loss vs steps for both to illustrate stability?

questions.title: What happens if we quantize the LM head to ternary as well?
questions.question_body: Often the final projection (hidden-to-vocab) is sensitive. You mention embeddings remain full precision; what about the LM head? Have you tried making the output projection ternary? How much perplexity degradation occurs, and would an 8-bit head be a better compromise?

questions.title: How does this approach differ from post-training quantization (PTQ) to 2–3 bits?
questions.question_body: The paper argues PTQ is sub-optimal and trains from scratch with ternary weights. Could you quantify the gap versus the best PTQ methods at 2–3 bits (e.g., with per-channel scales and GPTQ/AWQ-like error compensation)? Is the main advantage better optimization (weights learn to be ternary) or architectural changes (e.g., removal of biases, RMSNorm, symmetric activation quant)?

questions.title: Does the inclusion of zero in the ternary set explicitly improve "feature filtering"?
questions.question_body: The paper claims modeling capability is stronger because weights can be 0, enabling explicit feature filtering. Do you have evidence (e.g., sparsity patterns or ablations) showing that zero weights tend to prune redundant channels/features and improve downstream accuracy compared to purely binary {−1, +1} weights?

questions.title: What is the end-to-end energy model including memory traffic?
questions.question_body: Arithmetic energy is only part of total energy. For end-to-end inference, how do memory bandwidth and DRAM/SRAM transfers compare between 1.58-bit and FP16, especially for large models with pipeline/tensor parallelism? Do you account for packing/unpacking ternary weights and any overheads in real deployments?

questions.title: How does BitNet b1.58 handle long-context inference beyond 8-bit KV caches?
questions.question_body: You state activations are 8-bit and that this enables doubling context length. You also suggest lossless compression to 4 bits or lower for 1.58-bit LLMs as future work. Is there a scheme to store K/V at 4 bits without accuracy loss (e.g., per-head scaling with blockwise quantization)? How does per-token scaling complicate this for cached keys/values?

questions.title: In the 2T-token experiment vs StableLM-3B, what exactly differs?
questions.question_body: The 2T-token training follows StableLM-3B's data recipe, but model architecture, precision, and training dynamics differ. Are optimizer, LR schedule, and data mixing ratios identical? Since the parameter counts might differ, how do you attribute the improvements—precision, architecture tweaks, or size?

questions.title: How well does BitNet b1.58 map to CPUs and edge NPUs in practice?
questions.question_body: The paper claims 1.58-bit LLMs are CPU-friendly. Modern CPUs have fast INT8 dot-product (e.g., AVX-512 VNNI) but still perform multiplies. Do you have actual benchmarks on CPUs or edge NPUs showing speed/energy gains from using ternary weights with add/sub operations? Are there existing instruction sets that exploit ternary encoding efficiently?

questions.title: Could stochastic or learned thresholds improve ternary quantization over RoundClip?
questions.question_body: RoundClip after dividing by absmean implicitly sets thresholds at ±0.5 for mapping to {−1, 0, +1}. Have you tried learned thresholds or stochastic quantization to control the density of zeros per layer? Does tuning thresholds per-channel yield better accuracy without hurting the simple hardware story?
